```{r m2-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.8, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%")
```

With one criterion, a grading trades expected wrong-direction errors against
the cost of leaving pairs unordered. With two or more criteria—such as school
absence and suspension, race and gender contact gaps, or county income and
incarceration—you also have to decide what a directional error means. Averaging
wrong-direction errors across criteria and ordering a single composite index
are different decision problems that can favor opposite rankings even when all
target values are known.

This article extends the single-criterion loss from
[Posterior ranking, integer grades, and reporting loss](m1-ranking-and-loss.html)
to multiple criteria, contrasts weighted directional loss with a scalar
composite target, shows what posterior dependence each objective needs, and
examines the criterion-specific cost of sharing one common grading. Executed
chunks use direct arithmetic, stored `postrank_example()` objects, and two
fixed-order dynamic-programming cut examples (`postrank_cuts()`), so rendering
needs no external LP or MIP solver.

## Criterion-weighted loss {#one-report-several-error-counts}

Orient every criterion \(k \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) before grading so that larger
values of \(\theta_{ik}\) receive higher priority. A common grading assigns one
integer grade \(g_i \in \{1, \dots, G\}\) to each entity \(i\): **Grade 1 has
the highest priority**, \(x_{ij}(g) = \mathbf{1}\{g_i < g_j\}\) marks pairs
reported with \(i\) ahead of \(j\), \(M = \binom{n}{2}\) is the number of
unordered pairs, and \(N(g) = \sum_{i \ne j} x_{ij}(g)\) is the number of
ordered (`disclosed`) pairs. Entities in the same grade are left unordered.

On criterion \(k\), let \(e_{ij,k} = \Pr(\theta_{ik} \le \theta_{jk})\) be the
posterior probability that reporting \(i\) ahead of \(j\) is wrong, and let

\[
E_k(g) = \sum_{i \ne j} x_{ij}(g) \, e_{ij,k}
\]

be the posterior expected number of wrong-direction pairs on criterion \(k\).
All examples in this article assume zero posterior probability of exact ties
within each criterion; see
[Exact ties in the posterior versus withheld comparisons](m4-ties-and-withholding.html)
when exact equality has positive probability.

Choose criterion weights \(w = (w_1, \dots, w_K)\). In `postrank()` and
`postrank_settings()`, weights follow three rules:

1. Every weight must be finite and nonnegative (\(w_k \ge 0\)). A criterion can
   receive weight `0` so its error profile is tracked (or constrained by an
   error budget `q`) without entering the weighted objective.
2. Weights must sum to `1` within `1e-12`. **`postrank` never rescales weights
   automatically**; weights that do not sum to `1` stop with an error.
3. With two or more criteria, `weights` (or `settings`) must be supplied; only
   for a single criterion does `postrank()` fill in weight `1` when `weights`
   is omitted (`postrank_settings()` always requires `weights`). Named weights
   match criterion IDs, while unnamed weights in `postrank()` and
   `postrank_settings()` match the input's criterion order (passing `weights`
   directly to `postrank_problem()` or `postrank_evaluate()` requires criterion
   names).

Given weights \(w\) and withholding cost \(\tau \in (0, 1/2]\), each criterion
has its own loss \(R_k(g) = [E_k(g) + \tau\{M - N(g)\}]/M\), and the
criterion-weighted posterior expected loss is

\[
R_{w,\tau}(g)
= \frac{\sum_{k=1}^K w_k \, E_k(g) + \tau\{M - N(g)\}}{M}
= \tau + \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i \ne j} x_{ij}(g)
  \left(\sum_{k=1}^K w_k \, e_{ij,k} - \tau\right).
\]

Leaving a pair unordered costs \(\tau\) **once**, regardless of \(K\): the
weights average the directional-error probabilities across criteria rather than
multiplying \(\tau\) by \(K\). Setting \(K = 1\) and \(w_1 = 1\) recovers the
single-criterion loss, and giving every entity Grade 1 still has loss \(\tau\).

By linearity of expectation, \(R_{w,\tau}(g)\) holds whether criteria or entity
pairs are dependent or independent in the posterior. It does not assume that
errors are independent across criteria, nor does it mean that an ordered pair
is simultaneously right on every criterion. See Lee (2026), Chapter 11,
[Weighted directional risk from a supplied selection law](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#sec-weighted-directional-risk).

Criterion weights express how you trade wrong-direction errors on one criterion
against wrong-direction errors on another; they are not estimated from the
posterior. Giving two criteria equal weight (`0.5` and `0.5`) does not force
their expected error rates `E_over_N` to be equal. Bounding individual
criterion errors or minimizing the worst criterion's loss requires `q` or
`objective = "minimax"`, discussed below and in
[Computing grades, choosing settings, and reading solver bounds](m5-computing-grades.html).

## Why weighted loss differs from a composite target {#why-a-composite-is-a-different-target}

A linear composite defines a single combined target per entity, such as
\(c_i = \sum_{k=1}^K a_k \theta_{ik}\), and evaluates wrong-direction
probability as \(\Pr(c_i \le c_j)\). That probability depends on cardinal
differences across criteria, whereas \(\sum_{k=1}^K w_k e_{ij,k}\) averages
criterion-by-criterion ordering errors. Setting \(a = w\) does not make the two
objectives agree.

Even with zero posterior uncertainty, the two goals can rank a pair in opposite
orders. Suppose entity `A` has known targets \((1, -2)\) and entity `B` has
known targets \((0, 0)\):

- Under criterion-weighted loss with weights \(w = (3/4, 1/4)\) and
  \(\tau = 0.3\), reporting `A` ahead of `B` is right on criterion 1 and wrong
  on criterion 2 (loss \(1/4 = 0.25\)), reporting `B` ahead of `A` costs
  \(3/4 = 0.75\), and leaving the pair unordered costs \(0.30\). The best action
  reports **`A` ahead of `B`**.
- Under an equally weighted composite \(c_i = 0.5 \, \theta_{i1} + 0.5 \, \theta_{i2}\),
  \(c_A = -0.5 < c_B = 0\), so the composite orders **`B` ahead of `A`**.
  (Even with composite weights \(a = (3/4, 1/4)\), \(c_A = 3/4 - 2/4 = +0.25\),
  whereas changing `A` to \((1, -4)\) gives \(c_A = -0.25 < 0\) while keeping
  the criterion-weighted error of `A` ahead of `B` equal to \(1/4\).)

The disagreement comes from the definition of the target, not from estimation
noise; see Lee (2026), Chapter 12,
[Composite and criterion-specific reporting targets](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/12-conflict-estimands.html#sec-two-estimands).
The two losses agree in general only under strong alignment—for example, when
all positive-weight criteria share the exact same strict ordering across
entities in almost every posterior draw, which is much stronger than positive
correlation across criteria.

## Posterior information required across criteria {#which-posterior-information-is-needed}

To evaluate \(R_{w,\tau}(g)\), `postrank` needs only the within-criterion
pairwise probabilities \(e_{ij,k} = \Pr(\theta_{ik} \le \theta_{jk})\). Once
each \(e_{ij,k}\) is computed from the joint distribution of entities within
criterion \(k\), dependence *between* criteria does not change \(R_{w,\tau}(g)\).
(Within each criterion, dependence *between entities* still matters whenever
marginal intervals are converted to pairwise probabilities.)

Ordering a composite \(c_i = \sum_k a_k \theta_{ik}\)—or computing the
probability that `A` beats `B` on *both* criteria at once—does depend on how
the criteria move together within each entity. To see this directly, fix entity
`B` at \((0, 0)\) and compare two two-state distributions for entity `A` in
which each row has probability `1/2`:

```{r m2-two-laws}
library(postrank)

together <- rbind(c(2, 2), c(-1, -1))
opposite <- rbind(c(2, -1), c(-1, 2))
w <- c(0.5, 0.5)

law_summary <- function(A) {
  crit_err <- colMeans(A <= 0)
  c(crit_1 = crit_err[1], crit_2 = crit_err[2],
    weighted_error = sum(w * crit_err),
    composite_error = mean(as.vector(A %*% w) <= 0),
    correct_on_both = mean(rowSums(A > 0) == 2L))
}
rbind(together = law_summary(together), opposite = law_summary(opposite))
```

Both distributions have identical marginal error probabilities (`0.5` on
criterion 1 and `0.5` on criterion 2), so reporting `A` ahead of `B` has
criterion-weighted error `0.5` under both laws; at \(\tau = 0.2\), leaving the
pair unordered minimizes \(R_{w,\tau}\) under both laws. Under `opposite`,
however, \(c_A = 0.5(2) + 0.5(-1) = +0.5 > 0\) in every state, so reporting `A`
ahead of `B` has composite error `0` (while simultaneous correctness on both
criteria drops from `0.5` to `0`). Criterion-by-criterion probability tables
cannot distinguish `together` from `opposite`; see Lee (2026), Chapter 11,
[Exact comparison of additive, composite, and joint-event information](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#an-exact-information-boundary-example).

If your goal is to grade entities on a composite \(c_i\), compute \(c_i\) on
each joint posterior draw \(s\) before calling `postrank_draws()`, so
cross-criterion dependence is preserved. Combine values only when the draw IDs
identify the same joint state, whether the states were sampled independently
or by MCMC. Row numbers from separate fits do not establish this correspondence.
`postrank_composite()` computes a deterministic score vector from
posterior means using user-supplied `centers` and `scales`—useful for building
a fixed-order baseline, not a posterior distribution for \(c_i\). See
[Posterior representations and pairwise comparison probabilities](m3-posterior-inputs.html).

## Scale changes affect the two goals differently

Applying the same strictly increasing transformation to every entity on
criterion \(k\) preserves \(\theta_{ik} \le \theta_{jk}\) in every posterior
state. When the posterior is transformed directly and `weights`, `tau`, and the
allowed grade family are held fixed, \(e_{ij,k}\), \(R_{w,\tau}(g)\), and the
entire set of optimal gradings are unchanged.

A linear composite \(c_i = \sum_k a_k \theta_{ik}\) is not invariant to
nonlinear monotone transformations (or to rescaling one criterion while holding
\(a_k\) fixed). Likewise, refitting a statistical model after transforming an
outcome can change the posterior itself, and recomputing posterior means on a
transformed scale can change a mean-based baseline order; see Lee (2026),
Chapter 12,
[Ordinal invariance and qualified dominance statements](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/12-conflict-estimands.html#sec-invariance-dominance).

## Criterion-specific cost of a common grading and minimax {#read-the-burden-on-each-criterion}

The six fictional sites from
[Getting started: grading with one or two criteria](a1-getting-started.html)
illustrate how one common grading distributes expected errors across criteria.
We load the stored single-criterion, two-criterion, and commonality results:

```{r m2-load-tutorial}
one <- postrank_example("tutorial_one")
two <- postrank_example("tutorial_two")
commonality <- postrank_example("tutorial_commonality")
get_profile(two)[, c("criterion", "weight", "E", "E_over_N", "risk")]
```

With equal weights (`0.5` and `0.5`), `tau = 0.2`, and `G_max = 3`, the common
grading orders `N = 9` of the `15` site pairs. Its expected wrong-direction
rate among ordered pairs (`E_over_N`) is `0.0177` (`1.77%`) on `score_A` and
`0.0267` (`2.67%`) on `score_B`: equal weights in the objective do not force
equal criterion error rates.

Writing each criterion's loss as \(R_k(g) = [E_k(g) + \tau\{M - N(g)\}]/M\) gives
\(R_{w,\tau}(g) = \sum_{k=1}^K w_k R_k(g)\). Relative to the best grading chosen
for criterion \(k\) alone over the allowed family \(\mathcal{F}\), sharing the
common grading \(g_{\mathrm{common}}\) costs criterion \(k\) an extra loss of

\[
\Delta_k = R_k(g_{\mathrm{common}}) - \min_{h \in \mathcal{F}} R_k(h).
\]

Whenever \(g_{\mathrm{common}} \in \mathcal{F}\), \(\Delta_k \ge 0\).
`postrank_commonality_cost()` solves each criterion's own problem at the same
`tau`, `G_max`, and `exact_G`. If the common problem includes per-criterion
error budgets `q`, `protection = "drop"` (the default) solves each own-criterion
problem without `q`, while `protection = "keep"` retains all `q` error-budget
constraints from the common problem (even on criteria whose single-criterion
weight is `0`, so the common grading remains feasible in every single-criterion
solve). Computing `postrank_commonality_cost()` from scratch requires an
optimization solver—either the free `highs` package
(`install.packages("highs")` with `backend = "highs"` or
`options(postrank.backend = "highs")`) or a licensed Gurobi installation (the
default)—so the solver call below is shown without running during vignette
builds:

```{r m2-commonality-call, eval=FALSE}
commonality <- postrank_commonality_cost(
  two, backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(time_limit = 60, threads = 1, seed = 1304)
)
```

```{r m2-commonality-table}
commonality[["table"]][, c("criterion_id", "common_grade_risk",
  "own_best_risk", "cost_lower", "cost_upper")]
```

```{r m2-commonality, fig.cap="Extra loss per criterion from sharing one common grading across the six tutorial sites, with solver lower and upper bounds on each difference.", fig.alt="Horizontal plot of extra criterion loss for score_A (about 0.049) and score_B (about 0.014) when using the two-criterion common grading instead of each criterion's own optimal grading."}
postrank_plot_commonality(commonality)
```

Sharing the common grading adds `0.0490` loss units on `score_A` (`0.0906` vs.
`0.0417` alone) and `0.0145` on `score_B` (`0.0960` vs. `0.0816` alone). Both
differences combine wrong-direction errors and withheld pairs under the same
`tau = 0.2`. If an own-criterion solve returns checked loss \(U_k\) (the best
grading found) and solver lower bound \(L_k\) (a loss no grading in
\(\mathcal{F}\) can beat), `cost_lower` is
\(\max\{0, R_k(g_{\mathrm{common}}) - U_k\}\) and `cost_upper` is
\(R_k(g_{\mathrm{common}}) - L_k\); here both own-criterion solves are optimal,
so the two endpoints coincide. With a single criterion (`K = 1`), the common
and own-criterion problems are identical.

On the larger 30-site, three-criterion synthetic example (`pr_example_draws`,
criteria `poverty`, `frl`, and `snap` with weights `0.50`, `0.25`, and `0.25`
and `G_max = 4`), `snap` conflicts with the ordering of the other two criteria
and absorbs the largest extra loss under the shared four-grade report at
`tau = 0.35`:

```{r m2-commonality-30x3, fig.cap="Criterion-specific extra loss from sharing one common four-grade report across 30 synthetic sites on poverty, frl, and snap at tau = 0.35.", fig.alt="Horizontal interval plot of extra criterion loss across poverty, frl, and snap, with snap showing the largest extra loss."}
a35 <- postrank_example("analysis_30x3_tau35")
cc35 <- postrank_example("commonality_30x3_tau35")
cc35[["table"]][, c("criterion_id", "common_grade_risk", "own_best_risk",
  "own_lower_bound", "cost_lower", "cost_upper")]
postrank_plot_commonality(cc35)
```

That table records the consequences of the chosen weights without deciding
whether those weights are substantively right for an application. Lowering
`tau` to `0.25` on the same posterior (`analysis_30x3` and `commonality_30x3`)
makes leaving pairs unordered cheaper than resolving cross-criterion conflict,
so the common grading withholds every pair (`1` grade, `N = 0`—a valid
one-grade decision rather than a failed solver run, and not comparable by raw
loss value to `tau = 0.35` because changing `tau` changes the loss), even though
each criterion optimized on its own would still order pairs:

```{r m2-commonality-all-tie}
a25 <- postrank_example("analysis_30x3")
cc25 <- postrank_example("commonality_30x3")
c(common_grades = length(unique(get_grades(a25))),
  common_ordered_pairs = a25[["evaluation"]][["N"]])
cc25[["table"]][, c("criterion_id", "common_grade_risk", "own_best_risk",
  "own_G", "own_disclosures")]
```

When you want to protect the worst-performing criterion rather than minimize a
weighted average, set `objective = "minimax"` in `postrank()` or
`postrank_settings()`. Minimax minimizes

\[
\max_{k \in S} R_k(g)
\]

over the criterion subset `minimax_criteria` (all criteria by default)—the
largest **posterior expected** criterion loss, not the expectation of a
draw-by-draw maximum across criteria. By default (`minimax_refine = "weighted"`),
a second solver pass then minimizes \(R_{w,\tau}(g)\) among gradings that keep
the selected criteria at or below the first-stage minimax value; see
[Computing grades, choosing settings, and reading solver bounds](m5-computing-grades.html)
for an example using `postrank_example("toy_minimax")`.

## Fixed score-order cuts and comparing gradings under one loss {#separate-a-score-order-from-the-loss-it-is-evaluated-on}

A simpler baseline orders entities by a scalar score—such as weighted posterior
expected ranks from `postrank_expected_rank()` or a mean index from
`postrank_composite()`—and then partitions that fixed order into at most `G_max`
contiguous grades using `postrank_cuts()`. Even when `postrank_composite()`
builds the order, `postrank_cuts(..., rule = "optimal")` chooses cutpoints by
dynamic programming to minimize the **criterion-weighted** loss \(R_{w,\tau}(g)\)
along that order rather than evaluating composite-target error probabilities or
arbitrary equal-sized bins:

```{r m2-baselines-30x3}
er <- postrank_expected_rank(a35[["pairwise"]], a35[["settings"]][["weights"]])
head(sort(er))
er_cuts <- postrank_cuts(er, a35[["pairwise"]], a35[["settings"]])
er_cuts
means <- postrank_posterior_means(pr_example_draws)
comp <- postrank_composite(
  means, a35[["settings"]][["weights"]],
  scales = c(poverty = 1, frl = 1, snap = 1),
  centers = c(poverty = 0, frl = 0, snap = 0)
)
postrank_cuts(comp, a35[["pairwise"]], a35[["settings"]], direction = "descending")
```

In `postrank_composite()`, `centers` and `scales` are user-declared constants
rather than data-estimated standardizations: named vectors match criterion IDs
in any order and must list each criterion once, whereas an unnamed scalar is
recycled across criteria (missing, extra, or duplicate names stop with an
error). With quantile cuts (`rule = "quantile"`, `G_b`), entities with identical
scores are never split across grades, and the realized grade count must still
satisfy `G_max` and `exact_G`.

Because a baseline searches only contiguous cuts of its fixed score order, its
optimality scope is that order alone (with no whole-family LP/MIP lower bound or
gap). Every contiguous partition of a score order is also a valid integer
grading, so exact unrestricted optimization over \(\mathcal{F}\) achieves a loss
no larger than any fixed-order cut rule inside \(\mathcal{F}\) on the same
posterior and loss—whether that inequality is strict depends on the dataset, and
whether a numerical solver run reached the exact minimum depends on its status
and gap. See Lee (2026), Chapter 22,
[Conditional Bayes dominance and its limits](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/22-evaluation-frontiers.html#sec-conditional-bayes-dominance).

`postrank_compare()` evaluates the joint grading and fixed-order baselines on
one shared posterior and policy:

```{r m2-compare-30x3, fig.cap="Loss, ordered pairs, and occupied grades for the joint common grading and the expected-rank and composite fixed-order baselines on the 30-site example at tau = 0.35.", fig.alt="Comparison plot showing equal loss, ordered pair counts, and grade counts across the joint grading, expected-rank cuts, and composite cuts."}
cmp35 <- postrank_example("comparison_30x3_tau35")
cmp35[["table"]][, c("method", "risk", "N", "G", "status",
  "optimality_scope", "risk_absolute_gap", "family_feasible", "feasibility_reason")]
postrank_plot_compare(cmp35)
```

In `cmp35$table`, `status`, `optimality_scope`, and `reason` stay separate (any
row without a checked grading retains its status and reason without plotting a
grade), while `family_feasible` and `feasibility_reason` check `G_max`,
`exact_G`, and `q` within `cmp35$provenance$family_feasibility_tolerance`
(older saved comparisons without those columns display `"not recorded"` without
recomputing). On this 30-site example at `tau = 0.35`, all three rules choose
the same grading—so `postrank_plot_compare(cmp35, view = "relations")` and the
pairwise change map `postrank_plot_relations(a35, y = er_cuts, labels = "none")`
show zero changed pair relations—though agreement on one dataset does not imply
general equivalence:

```{r m2-change-map-30x3, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Pairwise ordering changes between the joint common grading and the expected-rank cut baseline on the 30-site example (all zero differences here).", fig.alt="Thirty-by-thirty relation-change matrix showing no changed pair relations between the joint grading and expected-rank cuts."}
postrank_plot_relations(a35, y = er_cuts, labels = "none")
```

To compare any externally chosen grading—such as the single-criterion `score_A`
grades on the six tutorial sites—against `two` under the two-criterion loss
without running baseline cut searches, pass named grade vectors to
`postrank_compare()` with `baselines = character()`:

```{r m2-same-loss}
comparison <- postrank_compare(
  two,
  `Score A grades` = get_grades(one),
  baselines = character()
)
comparison[["table"]][, c("method", "risk", "N", "G", "status")]
```

Evaluated on both criteria (`weights = c(0.5, 0.5)`, `tau = 0.2`), the
`score_A`-only grading orders `12` pairs and has two-criterion loss `0.1356`,
compared with `9` ordered pairs and loss `0.0933` for the common grading `two`.
Both gradings use `3` grades (`G_max = 3`), and both losses are evaluated under
the exact same two-criterion objective rather than comparing `one`'s
one-criterion loss directly against `two`'s two-criterion loss. Lower loss under
one chosen objective and posterior does not make a grading superior under a
different loss, target definition, or population distribution; see
[Figures and sensitivity to reporting settings](a7-figures-sensitivity.html)
for systematic sensitivity checks across weights, `tau`, and `G_max`.

## References

Lee, JoonHo (2026). *Decisions from Noisy Multidimensional Indicators: Theory,
Evidence, and Posterior Grading*. Companion book
(`citation("postrank")`; online Chapters 11, 12, and 22 in the expanded online
edition linked above). See also `?postrank_settings`,
`?postrank_commonality_cost`, and `?postrank_compare`.
